block.heading: A minimum wage on a diagram
block.text:
With guards' equilibrium at N$25 an hour and 400 jobs, a N$30 minimum wage cuts jobs to 300 while 500 want work: an excess labour supply of 200 in this competitive model.

![Minimum wage diagram](diagrams/item-6145-6.3-019-proc-answer.png)

item.prompt: In a competitive labour market for security guards, firms want 500, 400, 300 and 200 guards at wages of N$20, N$25, N$30 and N$35 an hour, and 300, 400, 500 and 600 people are willing to work as guards at those wages, as in the diagram. The government sets a minimum wage of N$30 an hour. Use the diagram to show the original equilibrium, the minimum wage and its effect in this model (4).
item.canonical_answer: In this competitive model the original equilibrium E, where labour demand D meets labour supply S, is N$25 an hour and 400 guards. Draw the minimum wage as a horizontal line at N$30, above the equilibrium wage, so it is binding. Neither curve shifts: at N$30 firms want 300 guards (read off D) and 500 people want to work as guards (read off S), an excess supply of labour of 200. Employment falls from 400 to 300, so there are 100 fewer jobs, while the 300 still employed earn N$5 an hour more. The result depends on the model: a minimum wage below N$25 would not bind, and outside the competitive model this diagram alone does not establish the employment response.
